lyrics:
Every day I catch myself
Is it me that is following
Or am I in step with my own tune
At my own pace
Aligned with the cosmos
Defining the course
And not standing still
Please tell me I'm flying
Even if it's wandering
If it's a detour, let it be
I'm moving, I'm moving
No map, no name, still it's me
Still it's me choosing
Every day I catch myself
Am I building something new
Or just rearranging the furniture
In a room I know too well
Trying to find a fresh view
From the same four four walls
Hoping for a breakthrough
Please tell me I'm flying
Even if it's wandering
If it's a detour, let it be
I'm moving, I'm moving
No map, no name, still it's me
Still it's me choosing
Every day I catch myself
On the 6:12 with my bag half-zipped
Listening to the brakes sigh at the stop
Checking my reflection in the dark window
Still wondering if I chose this route
Or if the route chose me
Either way, I'm moving
Please tell me I'm flying
Even if it's wandering
If it's a detour, let it be
I'm moving, I'm moving
No map, no name, still it's me
Still it's me choosing
Maybe the map is all a rumor
Maybe I’m learning as I go
One hand on the rail, one on the hour
Let it shift, let it show
If it's a detour, let it be
I'm moving, I'm moving
No map, no name, still it's me
Still it's me choosing

style: Experimental art rock with shifting BPM at every section change, led by interlocking electric guitar over fretless bass, double-kick drums, electronic-keyboard ostinatos, clipped alto sax multiphonics, and marimba patterns; asymmetrical meters, angular riffs, abrupt stop-start edits, tape saturation, granular delays, and an alto male vocal with tightly measured phrasing and uniform line lengths.

  Approved critic summary: Rose opens with a mumbled false start on 'I'm Old Now,' and that small, deliberate stumble tells you exactly what kind of record this is: nothing performed, nothing smoothed over, just a man taking honest stock.

  Approved critic summary: "A Distant Memory" opens with a counted-off "one, two, three, four" that sets a brisk 4/4 in C major, and from there Rose lets a female vocal float above a clean, roomy groove that leans more toward jazzy indie-pop than any straight ballad.

  Approved critic summary: There's a bat by the bed in this one, his father's before him, and nobody in the family has ever swung it.

  Approved critic summary: Nearly seven minutes, and Rose earns every one of them here by treating silence itself as the subject.

  Approved critic summary: For a songwriter introduced as a diarist, a philosopher of the ordinary who finds a lifetime in a reflection on a phone screen, "Outlandia" is a startling pivot: a two-hour rock opera, twenty-four scenes long, about how a country is bought, broken, and inventoried.
- 2026-08-20 — Them Bones (single)
  Approved critic summary: After the two-hour sprawl of "Outlandia," Rose narrows the lens back down to something you can hold in one hand, and "Them Bones" benefits from the compression.

  Approved critic summary: Rose builds this one on a 3/4 pulse at a brisk clip, which is the first surprise: a waltz that never asks you to sway, driven instead by a Hammond groove and gritty guitar working against the meter rather than settling into it.

impression.text: This upbeat pop-rock anthem establishes a bright, optimistic texture driven by energetic electric guitars and a driving rhythm section. The track maintains a highly propulsive energy level from start to finish, creating an uplifting and motivational feel. Its production is dense but expertly balanced, allowing crisp guitar riffs and vibrant synths to sit comfortably beneath the clear, upfront lead vocals. A defining quality of the song is the soaring guitar solo section, which adds an exciting melodic peak before seamlessly transitioning back into the triumphant, hook-heavy final chorus.

review.review_text: The title promises something knottier than what lands, and that gap is the story of this one: an art-rock brief built on shifting meters and clipped sax multiphonics that resolves, in the audio, into a bright and propulsive E-major push at a mid-tempo 89 BPM. What survives the translation is Rose's gift for the small confessional image. The best verse puts you on the commute directly: 'On the 6:12 with my bag half-zipped / Listening to the brakes sigh at the stop,' and that sighing brake does more work than any angular riff could. The chorus turns on a nice piece of self-permission, 'If it's a detour, let it be / I'm moving, I'm moving,' and the guitar solo near the four-minute mark gives the final chorus a genuine lift, the same forward tilt Rose reached for on 'Nowhere But Up.' It doesn't earn its experimental framing so much as sidestep it into a clean, hook-forward anthem, and the 'rearranging the furniture' verse leans a touch on the nose next to that train-window sharpness. Not his strangest hour despite the name, but the writing keeps its footing and the momentum never sags. A dependable cut that does its job and does it well.
